newsitem.title: USA: Spring job opportunities to blossom - Manpower survey.
newsitem.headline: Spring job opportunities to blossom - Manpower survey.

text.p: Job applicants can expect more opportunities to bloom this spring than in the first quarter of the year, according to a quarterly Employment Outlook Survey conducted by Manpower Inc.

"These figures really show improvement in all geographic areas," said Mitchell Fromstein, Manpower's chief executive officer. "We think this (hiring trend) is going across all industries. It's there in manufacturing, in the service field, in finance and the insurance sector. It's pretty much across the board."

The Manpower survey of more than 16,000 businesses in 487 cities indicates that 28 percent plan new hiring in the second quarter of 1997. Six percent expect their employment rolls to decline, while 63 percent foresee no change and 3 percent are uncertain about their hiring plans for the spring.

Manpower said the latest survey represents a substantial increase from the first quarter and an improvement from the totals one year ago, when 26 percent of the companies asked planned staff additions, 8 percent planned job decreases, 63 percent said staffing levels would remain unchanged and 3 percent were undecided.

"I think companies just need people (now)," Fromstein said. "Hiring has continued pretty well for the last two or three years. A lot of it follows several years of downsizing or holding back on the hiring process."
While the latest upward hiring trend is widespread among industries, there are specific geographic areas that are showing faster growth than others, Fromstein said.
"The Southeast and Midwest are still the strongest growth areas," Fromstein said. "And the west coast, particularly California and southern California, is also really making a strong comeback."
Fromstein added that finding a job in the public sector remains a little tougher than in the private sector.

"The growth in public sector employment has slowed down over the last couple of years," he said. "I think it's probably (the result of) public pressure and budget pressure. It's coming back a little bit, but not like the private sector is."
